questions.stem: Which of these is an example of succession?
options: A moth population becoming darker over many generations in a polluted area
A flock of birds flying north each autumn and returning south each spring
A kangaroo population rising in wet years and falling again in dry years
Weeds, then shrubs, then trees colonising a cleared block over several decades
questions.explanation: Succession is the gradual change in the mix of species in an area over time, following a disturbance such as clearing. A moth population becoming darker is evolution by natural selection, seasonal movement is migration, and numbers rising and falling with rainfall is a population change within one species.

questions.stem: What distinguishes primary succession from secondary succession?
options: Primary succession involves only animals; secondary succession involves only plants
Primary succession takes a few weeks; secondary succession takes many thousands of years
Primary succession happens only in water; secondary succession happens only on land
Primary succession begins where there is no soil; secondary begins where soil remains
questions.explanation: Primary succession starts on newly formed or exposed surfaces with no soil, such as lava or bare rock. Secondary succession follows a disturbance that leaves the soil, and often seeds and roots, in place. Primary succession is usually much slower, because soil must form first.

questions.stem: A volcanic eruption forms a new island of bare lava in the ocean. Which organisms are most likely to colonise it first?
options: Predators such as hawks and large snakes
Pioneer species such as lichens and mosses
Large trees that need deep, moist, fertile soils
Grazing mammals that feed on grasses
questions.explanation: Pioneer species such as lichens, mosses and some hardy plants can survive on bare rock with few nutrients. They help weather the rock and add organic matter, starting soil formation. Trees, grazers and predators depend on soil, plants or prey that are not yet present.

questions.stem: Which sequence of communities is most likely on a new volcanic island over hundreds of years?
options: Lichens and mosses, then grasses and ferns, then shrubs, then trees
Trees, then shrubs, then grasses and ferns, then lichens and mosses
Grasses and ferns, then trees, then lichens and mosses, then shrubs
Shrubs, then lichens and mosses, then trees, then grasses and ferns
questions.explanation: Pioneer species such as lichens and mosses colonise bare rock first and begin forming soil. As soil deepens, grasses and ferns, then shrubs and finally trees can establish. Trees cannot grow first, because they need deep soil.

questions.stem: A bushfire burns a eucalypt forest. Within months, eucalypts resprout from buds under the bark and from lignotubers, and seedlings appear. What type of succession is this?
options: Secondary succession, because soil, roots and seeds survived the fire
Primary succession, because all the living plants above ground were burnt
Primary succession, because the forest must start again from bare rock
Secondary succession, because the fire created a new layer of lava rock
questions.explanation: A bushfire removes much of the vegetation but leaves soil, a seed bank and living roots and buds, so regrowth is secondary succession. Many Australian plants resprout or release seed after fire. Burnt plants above ground do not make it primary succession, because soil remains.

questions.stem: Two areas are disturbed in the same year: a paddock is abandoned by a farmer, and a glacier retreats to expose bare rock. Which prediction is best supported?
options: Neither area will change, as succession happens only after volcanic eruptions
The paddock will return to forest much faster, as soil and seeds are present
The bare rock will return to forest faster, as it has no competing weeds
Both areas will reach the same community in the same time, as climate is equal
questions.explanation: The abandoned paddock undergoes secondary succession, with soil and seeds already present, so it changes quickly. The exposed rock undergoes primary succession, which is slow because soil must first form. Succession follows many kinds of disturbance, not only eruptions.

questions.stem: Over many decades of succession after a disturbance, which trend is usually observed?
options: Soil depth and total biomass tend to increase as the community develops
Soil depth and total biomass tend to decrease as the community develops
The number of species stays fixed while the soil is washed away entirely
Pioneer species become more and more common until they replace all others
questions.explanation: As succession proceeds, soil deepens, larger plants establish and total biomass increases, until a relatively stable community develops. Pioneer species are usually replaced by later species as conditions change, rather than taking over.

questions.stem: What is meant by the climax community at the end of succession?
options: A relatively stable community that changes little until the next disturbance
The first community of pioneer species to colonise bare rock after a disturbance
A community made up of a single species that has replaced all of its competitors
The community present at the exact moment a fire or flood disturbs the area
questions.explanation: Succession continues until a relatively stable community develops, often called the climax community, which changes little until another disturbance. Pioneer species form the first community, not the last.

questions.stem: A new fungal disease kills 90% of a plantation of genetically identical trees but only 20% of a wild, genetically varied population of the same species. What does this show?
options: Genetically identical trees are unable to produce any immune response at all
A diverse gene pool is more likely to include alleles that allow survival
Plantations are always more exposed to fungal spores than wild forests are
The fungus caused resistance mutations in the wild trees but not the others
questions.explanation: When all individuals carry the same alleles, a new selection pressure affects them alike. A genetically varied population is more likely to include individuals with alleles for resistance, which survive and reproduce. The disease selects existing variation rather than causing helpful mutations.

questions.stem: Which species is a well-known example of a population with very low genetic diversity?
options: The European rabbit
The cheetah
The common brown rat
The house sparrow
questions.explanation: Cheetahs have very low genetic diversity, thought to be the result of past population bottlenecks. Rats, sparrows and rabbits have large, widespread populations with much more variation in their gene pools.

questions.stem: Skin grafts between unrelated cheetahs were often not rejected, although grafts between unrelated individuals of most mammal species are. What does this suggest?
options: Cheetahs are all clones produced by asexual reproduction in the wild
Cheetahs have more variation in immune genes than most other mammals
Cheetahs have very little variation in the genes for immune recognition
Cheetahs have no immune system, so they cannot reject any foreign tissue
questions.explanation: Grafts are rejected when the immune system recognises tissue as foreign, which depends on genes that are usually highly variable. Acceptance of grafts between unrelated cheetahs shows these genes are very similar across the population, a sign of low genetic diversity. Cheetahs do have immune systems and reproduce sexually.

questions.stem: Devil facial tumour disease is a cancer spread between Tasmanian devils when they bite each other. Why has it spread so easily through the population?
options: The disease is carried by a virus that infects all marsupials across Australia
Devils lost their immune systems after being isolated from the mainland
Low genetic diversity means devils' immune systems rarely recognise the tumour cells
High genetic diversity means the devils' immune systems attack their own healthy cells
questions.explanation: The tumour cells themselves are passed from devil to devil. Because devils are so genetically similar, especially in immune genes, the transferred cells are rarely recognised as foreign and are not rejected. The disease is caused by transmitted cancer cells, not a virus.

questions.stem: Why does inbreeding in a small, isolated population often lead to more offspring with inherited disorders?
options: Related parents always have offspring with new mutations that cause serious genetic diseases
Related parents pass on fewer chromosomes, so their offspring lack some genes
Related parents produce offspring with dominant alleles that cannot be expressed
Related parents are more likely to pass on two copies of the same harmful recessive allele
questions.explanation: Relatives share many alleles, so their offspring are more likely to be homozygous for harmful recessive alleles, which are then expressed. This lowers survival and reproduction and adds to extinction risk. Inbreeding does not change chromosome number or cause new mutations.

questions.stem: Zoos running a captive breeding program for a threatened species keep detailed records of each animal's ancestry. Why?
options: To pair animals that are closely related, so their offspring look the same
To make sure only one pair breeds, so the gene pool stays exactly the same
To choose animals with new mutations, so the species evolves more quickly
To pair animals that are unrelated, keeping as much genetic diversity as possible
questions.explanation: Breeding programs use ancestry records to pair unrelated animals, which avoids inbreeding and keeps as many alleles as possible in the captive population. Breeding close relatives would increase the expression of harmful recessive alleles, and relying on one pair would shrink the gene pool.

questions.stem: What is a population bottleneck?
options: A narrow strip of habitat that animals use to move between two larger patches
A sharp fall in population size that leaves few survivors and fewer alleles
A barrier such as a mountain range that splits one population into two parts
A rapid rise in population size when a species colonises a new, empty habitat
questions.explanation: In a bottleneck, an event such as disease, hunting or a natural disaster kills most of a population, and the survivors carry only some of the original alleles. Genetic diversity stays low even if numbers later recover. A narrow strip linking habitat patches is a corridor.

questions.stem: Which Australian tree, found in the wild only in a small area of New South Wales, is known for its extremely low genetic diversity?
options: The coastal banksia
The Wollemi pine
The river red gum
The mountain ash
questions.explanation: The Wollemi pine was discovered in 1994 in a remote gorge in the Blue Mountains region and has very few wild trees with almost no genetic variation between them, making it vulnerable to disease. River red gums, mountain ash and coastal banksias are widespread.

questions.stem: Which human activity is regarded as the greatest threat to species worldwide?
options: Light pollution from city street lights
Recreational bushwalking on marked tracks
Noise from traffic on country roads
Destruction and fragmentation of habitat
questions.explanation: Clearing land for farming, cities, mining and logging removes the food, shelter and breeding sites that species depend on, and splits the rest into small, isolated patches. Light, noise and recreation can disturb wildlife, but their effects are far smaller.

questions.stem: How does breaking a large forest into small, isolated patches increase extinction risk for the species living there?
options: Each patch increases the rate of gene flow, so the separate species merge into one
Each patch holds a small population, which loses diversity through drift and inbreeding
Each patch has more food than before, so the populations grow beyond what they can survive
Each patch forces all the species into one niche, so their alleles become identical
questions.explanation: Fragmentation turns one large population into several small ones with little gene flow between them. Small populations lose alleles through genetic drift and inbreeding and are more easily wiped out by a single fire or disease. Isolation reduces gene flow rather than increasing it.

questions.stem: Which group of introduced predators has contributed most to the extinction of small and medium-sized Australian mammals since European colonisation?
options: Cane toads and European carp
Rabbits and feral goats
Feral cats and red foxes
Dingoes and wedge-tailed eagles
questions.explanation: Feral cats and red foxes, introduced after European colonisation, prey on small and medium-sized native mammals and are regarded as the main cause of Australia's mammal extinctions in that time, together with habitat loss. Rabbits and goats harm native species mainly through competition and habitat damage, not predation.

questions.stem: Cane toads were introduced to Queensland in the 1930s and have spread across northern Australia. Why have numbers of some native predators, such as northern quolls, fallen sharply where toads arrive?
options: The toads eat all the quolls' young before they leave the den
The toads carry a virus that makes the predators unable to breed
The toads compete with quolls for the same burrows and nest hollows
The predators eat the toxic toads and many die from the poison
questions.explanation: Cane toads produce a toxin, and predators that attack or eat them, such as northern quolls and some goannas and snakes, often die. Native predators did not evolve with toads, so few individuals had behaviour or resistance to cope with this new selection pressure.

questions.stem: In a frog-eating snake species, individuals in areas where toxic cane toads have been present longest tend to have smaller heads relative to body length. Which explanation fits natural selection?
options: The toad toxin causes mutations that make each snake's head grow more slowly
Snakes in those areas decided to eat less, so their offspring had smaller heads
Snakes with smaller gapes cannot swallow the largest toads, so more survive to breed
Each snake shrinks its head during its lifetime so that it avoids eating toads
questions.explanation: A snake with a small gape cannot swallow a large toad carrying a lethal dose of toxin, so it is more likely to survive and pass on its alleles. Over generations, the average head size falls. The toxin acts as a selection pressure on existing variation rather than causing helpful mutations or changes within one lifetime.

questions.stem: The myxoma virus was released in Australia in 1950 to control rabbits. Within years, a much greater proportion of rabbits survived infection. What explains this?
options: Rabbits with alleles giving resistance survived and passed those alleles on
Rabbits that caught the virus became immune and passed that immunity to all offspring
Rabbits deliberately mutated their genes so that the virus could not infect them
Rabbits with resistance alleles were removed, leaving only the weaker rabbits
questions.explanation: The virus was a new selection pressure. Rabbits that happened to carry alleles giving resistance survived and reproduced, so resistance alleles became more common. Immunity gained by infection is not inherited, and mutations are not made on purpose.

questions.stem: Why is the overuse of antibiotics described as a human activity that creates a selection pressure?
options: It makes bacteria reproduce sexually, which mixes the resistance genes
It strengthens the human immune system so bacteria must evolve faster
It kills susceptible bacteria, so resistant bacteria survive and multiply
It causes every bacterium it comes into contact with to become resistant
questions.explanation: Antibiotics kill bacteria that are susceptible, leaving any with resistance alleles to survive and reproduce, so the frequency of resistance rises. The antibiotic selects existing resistant bacteria rather than making them resistant. Bacteria reproduce asexually.

questions.stem: Which human activity reduces biodiversity mainly by removing individuals faster than the population can replace them?
options: Planting wildlife corridors
Building seed banks
Setting up quarantine checks
Overfishing and overhunting
questions.explanation: Overexploitation, such as overfishing or overhunting, removes individuals faster than they can be replaced by reproduction, so populations shrink and can become extinct. Corridors, seed banks and quarantine are ways of protecting biodiversity.

questions.stem: Which human activity contributes most to climate change by adding carbon dioxide to the atmosphere?
options: Installing solar panels on house roofs
Burning fossil fuels such as coal, oil and gas
Growing native trees on degraded farmland soils
Generating electricity from wind turbines
questions.explanation: Burning fossil fuels releases carbon that has been stored underground for millions of years as carbon dioxide, an important greenhouse gas. Land clearing and some farming practices also add greenhouse gases. Planting trees removes carbon dioxide, and wind and solar generation produce little.

questions.stem: Which human activity contributes to climate change by releasing methane, a greenhouse gas?
options: Recycling paper and cardboard packaging
Raising large numbers of cattle and sheep
Planting forests on cleared farming land
Using solar power to heat household water
questions.explanation: Cattle and sheep produce methane as they digest grass, so large numbers of livestock add methane to the atmosphere. Planting forests removes carbon dioxide, and solar power and recycling reduce emissions rather than adding methane.

questions.stem: As the climate warms, a plant species that lives only near the summits of mountains is predicted to become extinct. Why is it especially at risk?
options: Its suitable habitat shifts uphill, and there is no higher ground left to move to
Warmer air causes its seeds to germinate in winter, so all its seedlings drown
Rising temperatures make the mountain summits taller, leaving it without soil
Warmer conditions stop all photosynthesis in plants growing at high altitude
questions.explanation: As temperatures rise, the conditions a cold-adapted species needs move to higher altitudes. A species already at the summit has nowhere further uphill to go, so its habitat shrinks and may disappear. Warming does not change the height of mountains or stop photosynthesis.

questions.stem: Why does a marine heatwave threaten the corals of the Great Barrier Reef?
options: High temperatures make corals grow so fast that their skeletons break apart
High temperatures cause the corals to produce too much oxygen, poisoning them
High temperatures cause corals to expel their algae, which can lead to starvation
High temperatures make the sea water too salty for the corals to take in any food
questions.explanation: Corals depend on symbiotic algae living in their tissues for much of their food. When the water stays too warm, corals expel the algae and turn white, which is coral bleaching. If high temperatures last, the corals can starve and die.

questions.stem: A species of frog has a short generation time and a large, genetically diverse population. A related frog has a long generation time and a small population. Which is more likely to survive rapid climate change?
options: The first, as variation and fast generations allow allele frequencies to change faster
The second, as long-lived individuals can choose to adapt during their own lifetimes
The first, as large populations are not affected by any change in the environment
The second, as small populations are protected from selection by genetic drift
questions.explanation: Natural selection needs variation, and change in allele frequencies happens between generations. A large, diverse population with short generations is more likely to contain suitable alleles and to increase their frequency quickly. Individuals cannot adapt genetically within a lifetime, and large populations are still affected by change.

questions.stem: The thylacine, or Tasmanian tiger, is extinct. Which combination of human activities contributed to its extinction in Tasmania?
options: Clearing of coral reefs, and the use of the myxoma virus
Introduction of the dingo, and rising ocean temperatures
Hunting encouraged by bounties, and the loss of its habitat
Overfishing of the rivers, and the spread of cane toads
questions.explanation: Thylacines were hunted in Tasmania, with bounties paid for killing them, and they also lost habitat as land was cleared for farming. Dingoes never reached Tasmania, and cane toads have not spread there.

questions.stem: Why are species on remote islands, such as New Zealand's flightless birds, often especially vulnerable to introduced predators?
options: Island species have larger populations, so predators can find them more easily
They evolved without such predators, so few have alleles for suitable defences
They evolved with more predators than mainland species, so they are already weak
Island species reproduce asexually, so they have no variation in their gene pools
questions.explanation: Species that evolved in isolation without mammalian predators often lack behaviours, such as wariness or fleeing, that would protect them, so a new predator is a strong selection pressure on a gene pool with little relevant variation. Island populations also tend to be small, not large, and they reproduce sexually.

questions.stem: Why do Australia's biosecurity and quarantine laws help protect native species?
options: They stop native animals breeding with each other so they keep their gene pools
They move native species overseas so they are safe from environmental change
They stop pests and diseases that could harm native species entering the country
They allow overseas animals to be released freely so they can boost biodiversity
questions.explanation: Quarantine and biosecurity laws restrict the entry of plants, animals, soil and other materials that could carry pests, weeds or diseases. Introduced species have already caused many extinctions in Australia, so preventing new arrivals protects native biodiversity.

questions.stem: Which conservation strategy stores the genetic diversity of plant species as a backup in case wild populations are lost?
options: A climax community
A selective herbicide
A seed bank
A food web
questions.explanation: Seed banks store seeds from many individuals and populations of plant species under cool, dry conditions, preserving a wide range of alleles. They can be used to restore populations if wild plants are lost.

questions.stem: How do wildlife corridors help to maintain biodiversity in fragmented habitats?
options: They link patches so animals can move between them, allowing gene flow
They stop animals moving between patches, keeping each gene pool separate
They replace native vegetation with crops, giving animals more food to eat
They remove predators from each patch, so prey species never need to move
questions.explanation: Corridors of native vegetation connect isolated patches, so individuals can move, find mates and recolonise areas. This allows gene flow, which increases genetic diversity and lowers the risk of local extinction.

questions.stem: Which argument for preventing extinction is an ethical argument based on the intrinsic value of species?
options: Native plants may contain chemicals that could be developed into new medicines
Healthy reefs and forests bring tourists who spend money in local towns
Insect pollinators are needed for many of the crops that humans depend on
Every species has a right to exist, whether or not it is useful to humans
questions.explanation: An intrinsic value argument holds that species are valuable in themselves and that humans have an obligation not to cause their extinction. Medicines, tourism and pollination are arguments based on the usefulness of species to humans.

questions.stem: Logging a native forest would bring jobs to a town but remove the main habitat of a threatened possum. Which statement best describes how science contributes to this decision?
options: Science cannot say anything useful about forests, so economics must decide alone
Science shows that jobs always matter more than any threatened species
Science can predict the effects on the possum, but values decide the outcome
Science can prove which choice is morally right, so no debate is needed
questions.explanation: Scientific data can estimate how logging would affect the possum population and its genetic diversity, but deciding between jobs and conservation also involves social, economic and ethical values. Science has limitations and cannot settle what people ought to choose.

questions.stem: Why is maintaining biodiversity described as having long-term biological and environmental consequences?
options: Losing species has no effect for thousands of years, so only future generations notice
Losing species is reversed naturally within a few generations through new mutations
Losing species can disrupt food webs and ecosystem services, and extinction cannot be undone
Losing species always increases the populations of all the remaining species in an ecosystem
questions.explanation: Each species interacts with others, so losing it can disrupt food webs, pollination, nutrient cycling and other services that ecosystems provide. An extinct species and its gene pool are lost permanently, so decisions made now affect the future.
